claims.text: The as-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure containing phases and interfaces at multiple length scales.
The proposed surrogate model integrates nanoprecipitate size, phase distribution, compositional gradients, and mechanical data as inputs.
High-resolution microstructural measurements and targeted in situ mechanical tests will be incorporated into training the surrogate model.
The surrogate will improve prediction accuracy for Young's modulus by 30–50% relative to continuum or single-scale simulations.
The surrogate will improve prediction accuracy for yield strength by 30–50% relative to continuum or single-scale simulations.
The surrogate will improve prediction accuracy for fracture resistance or related fracture metrics by 30–50% relative to continuum or single-scale simulations.
The surrogate will make predictions three- to five-fold faster than established continuum or single-scale simulations.
Local phase interfaces, compositional gradients, and nanoprecipitates provide hierarchical strengthening pathways in HfNbTiVAl10.
Representing heterogeneous strengthening and fracture processes at multiple length scales enables more accurate mapping from microstructure to mechanical response.
Conventional continuum models are less accurate because they lack the required multiscale microstructural resolution.
Established continuum or conventional finite-element simulations for multi-principal-element alloys generally omit hierarchical microstructural descriptors.
Applying the model to microstructures or loading conditions outside the training distribution can cause extrapolation errors.
Dynamic phase transformations can invalidate a model trained under static microstructural assumptions.
Rare or complex phase morphologies are inadequately represented in the current training database.
Validation will use new HfNbTiVAl10 samples with systematically varied precipitate fractions and heat-treatment paths.
Validation measurements will include stress–strain curves, crack-tip opening displacement, crack-growth rates, and local strain fields.
The hypothesis will be declared falsified if stress–strain or crack-growth measurements systematically fall outside pre-established 95% prediction bounds, even after retraining.
